## Methods

Ethical statement
All animal experimental procedures were approved by Cedars-Sinai Medical Center’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC 7611) and the ARVO Statement for the Use of Animals in Ophthalmic and Vision Research.

Animals
The Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rats were maintained in a 12 h light/dark cycle at 20–25°C and controlled humidity (30–70%) in a pathogen-free facility with ad libitum access to food and water. Both male and female rats were used for all experiments. The rats between postnatal day (P) 21-23 were randomly assigned to two groups: one group received a subretinal injection of human neural progenitors (hNPCs) (n=65), while the others served as untreated control (n=44). To minimize the immune response to human-derived cells in this xenograft model, cyclosporine A was administered via drinking water (210 mg/L), starting 1 day prior to transplantation and continuing until sacrifice. The experiment was repeated 3 times for P60 (untreated: n=24; hNPC-treated: n=30) and 2 times for P90 (untreated: n=20; hNPC-treated: n=35) time points.

Cell preparation and transplantation
The generation and expansion of hNPCs were conducted by Svendsen et al. in 199887. Briefly, human neural progenitor cells were isolated from the developing human cortex and grown in culture as sphere-shaped clusters. The spheres were sectioned into quarters, and cell-cell contacts were maintained. This simple and novel culture method allows rapid expansion of large numbers of hNPCs. Research-grade hNPCs were used in this study under the Stem Cell Research Oversight Committee (Pro00025772) at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center. Cells were prepared according to our published protocol20. Briefly, hNPC vials were rapidly thawed in a 37°C water bath after removal from liquid nitrogen, followed by resuspension in prewarmed Stemline medium (Sigma, St. Louis, Missouri) supplemented with rhEGF (100 ng/mL; Millipore, Billerica, MA) and rhLIF (100 ng/mL; Millipore). The cell suspension was centrifuged at 200 × g for 5 min, and the pellet was resuspended in Balanced salt solution (BSS, Alcon). Cells were then labeled using PKH26 Red Fluorescent Cell Linker Kits (Sigma, St. Louis, Missouri) according to the manufacturer’s protocol and finally resuspended at a concentration of 30,000 cells/μL in BSS. Cells were kept on ice until transplantation. Cell injections were performed following a previously established protocol20. Briefly, 2 μL of the hNPC suspension (6 × 10^4 cells/eye) was injected into the subretinal space of both left and right eyes through a small scleral incision using a fine glass pipette (internal diameter 75–150 μm) attached via tubing to a 25-μL syringe (Hamilton). To reduce intraocular pressure and minimize cell efflux, the cornea was punctured prior to injection. Immediately after injection, the fundus was examined for retinal damage or signs of vascular distress. Animals showing such issues were excluded from further study.

Efficacy evaluation
Optokinetic response (OKR). OKR testing provides a non-invasive method for assessing spatial visual acuity, measured in cycles per degree (c/d). Visual acuity was evaluated at P60 and P90, following our previously published protocol11,20. Animals were tested using a virtual reality–based OKR system consisting of an elevated circular platform surrounded by four computer monitors and a downward-facing overhead camera (OptoMotry HD, Cerebral Mechanics, Lethbridge, Canada). The monitors displayed rotating vertical grating patterns generated and controlled by OptoMotry HD software, with spatial frequencies ranging from 0.003 to 0.6 c/d. The movement of this grating induces an optokinetic response, where the rodents’ eyes and head track the movement involuntarily. Using the OKR OptoMotry system, measurements are limited to 0.6 c/d because reliability decreases at higher spatial frequencies. Due to lateralized visual processing and the rodent preference for temporal-to-nasal motion, each eye was assessed independently by presenting clockwise rotation to preferentially stimulate the left eye and counterclockwise rotation to stimulate the right eye. OKR testing was terminated when animals no longer exhibited tracking responses to the visual stimulus. The OKR results were observed and recorded by two independent, blinded investigators. Data were analyzed after incorporating our previous study datasets.

Electroretinography (ERG). Electroretinography (ERG) measures the overall electrical activity of the retina in response to light stimulation. ERG recordings were performed at P60 and P90 according to our previously established protocol19,20. In brief, following overnight (14–16 h) dark adaptation, animals were prepared under dim red light. Scotopic ERGs were recorded by stimulating the eyes with 5 ms white-light flashes at an intensity of 25 cd·s/m² with 10 s interstimulus intervals using a computer-controlled Espion system (Diagnosys LLC). A total of 20–30 sweeps were recorded for each animal, and the averaged responses were used to determine the response amplitude and assess rod-mediated retinal function. Data were analyzed after incorporating our previous study datasets.

Isolation of grafted hNPCs and rat retinal cells. Rats were sacrificed at P60 and P90 time points after visual function tests. Eyes were enucleated, and retinas were dissected in AMES solution (equilibrated with 95% O2/5% CO2). Under a fluorescent dissecting microscope, red fluorescent region containing the injection site (dorsal-temporal part) was dissected from the retina. For untreated retinas, the dorsal-temporal part corresponding to the same location in the cell-treated eye was dissected. Retinas from 8-15 rats were pooled, digested with papain, and dissociated into single-cell suspensions through manual trituration in ovomucoid solution88. Single-cell suspensions from hNPC-treated and untreated retinas were labeled with DAPI. PKH26-labeled hNPCs, along with hNPC-treated and untreated retinal cells, were sorted using a FACS sorter (FACSAria III, BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ) and collected into 1.7 mL RNase-free tubes (Eppendorf, Hamburg, Germany) containing 2% BSA in PBS. From hNPC-treated cell suspension, PKH26-labeled hNPCs and treated retinal cells were collected in separate tubes.

Single-cell RNA sequencing and library preparation. The sorted grafted hNPCs, rat retinal cell suspensions, and in vitro hNPCs were immediately processed for single-cell RNA sequencing following the 10x Chromium v3 single-cell reagent kit protocol for library preparation. cDNA library quantification and quality were assessed with D1000 or D5000 HS kit for the Agilent TapeStation 4200. Libraries were sequenced using Illumina Novaseq 6000 S4 platform using 100 bp paired-end sequencing for a sequencing depth of 50,000 read pairs/cell.

Histology and immunofluorescence staining. Eyes were enucleated from P60 and P90 time points, fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, and embedded in OCT for cryostat sections. Retinal cryostat sections were placed on a series of 5 slides, with 4 sections per slide. The first slide of each series was used for cresyl violet staining to visualize retinal lamination and donor cell location. The remaining slides were then used for immunofluorescent staining following previously described protocols20,89. Briefly, retinal sections were rehydrated in 1× PBS and blocked for 1 h in 2.5% BSA solution containing 5% serum (respective to the antibodies). Sections were incubated with primary antibodies at 4°C overnight with following antibodies: rabbit anti-MANF (1:200; Sigma, HPA011175), rabbit anti-MYDGF (1:200; Proteintech, 11353-1-AP), rabbit anti-KDELR (1:200; Thermo Fisher Scientific, PA5-101011), mouse anti-human nuclear marker (1:300; Millipore, MAB1281), goat anti-Iba1 (1:1000; FUJIFILM Wako Pure Chemical Corporation, 019-197441), goat anti-doublecortin (1:200; Santa Cruz Biotechnology, sc-8066), mouse anti-MAP2 (2a + 2b) (1:500; Sigma, M1406), mouse anti-RPE65 (1:500; Sigma, MAB5428), mouse anti-AQP4 (1:500; R&D Systems, MAB11659-SP), rabbit anti-collagen IV (1:200; Abcam, ab19808), mouse anti-tenascin C (1:500; Abcam, ab86182), rabbit anti-cone arrestin (1:1000; Millipore, AB15282), rabbit anti-GFAP (1:1000; Dako–Agilent, Z0334), rabbit anti-nestin (1:2000; Millipore, ABD69), rabbit anti-NCAM1 (1:200; Proteintech, 14255-1-AP), rabbit anti-IMPG2 (1:200; Abcam, ab272558), rabbit anti-oligodendrocyte-specific protein (1:100; Abcam, ab7474), rabbit anti-recoverin (1:2000; Millipore, AB5585), rabbit anti-SOX2 (D6D9) XP (1:400; Cell Signaling Technology, 3579), and rabbit anti-TXNL6 (1:200; Proteintech, 11203-1-AP). Following incubation with the primary antibodies, sections were washed three times for 5 min each in 1× PBS and incubated with anti-mouse or -rabbit or -goat secondary antibodies conjugated to Alexa Fluor-488 or Alexa Fluor-568 for 1 h at room temperature. Sections were counterstained with 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI) and mounted using Fluorescent Mount media (Sigma-Aldrich). Images were taken with a Leica or Nikon microscope.

Image analysis. Differences in immunoreactivity of MANF, Col IV, IMPG2, and NCAM1 between untreated and hNPC-treated retina at P60 and P90 were assessed as fluorescent intensities (FI) with our previous protocol88. In brief, for FI measurements, MANF, Col IV, IMPG2, and NCAM1 positive region of interest (ROI) was selected using ImageJ freehand tool. Fluorescent intensities of ROIs were measured after normalizing to the background. Fluorescent intensity values were averaged (4 sections per retina and 8-9 retinas per group; each section 40 μm apart) to determine signal density. The FI values were presented as arbitrary units. The processing and analysis were kept consistent between images. Statistical analysis was performed on average FI values (mean ± SEM). MANF+ microglia were counted manually (4 sections per retina and 10 retinas per group; each section 40 μm apart). Image analysis was performed blindly and separately by 2 observers.

Preliminary processing scRNA-seq raw data of hNPCs and retinal cells. Cell Ranger software (version 4.0.0) (https://support.10xgenomics.com/single-cell-gene-expression/software/pipelines/4.0/what-is-cell-ranger) was used to perform preliminary processing of single-cell sequencing data, including aligning sequencing reads to the reference transcriptome (hNPCs: GRCh38; rat: Rnor6), estimating and filtering, and generating feature-barcode matrices. Wild-type rat sequencing data from Wang et al. were downloaded from the GEO database (GSE209872: GSM6403183 and GSM6403184).

Removing low-quality cells and identification of cell types. Seurat (version 4.4.0) software was used to perform downstream quality control, integration, identification of cell types, and subsequent differential expression gene analysis on the gene-cell expression matrices obtained above90. For hNPC datasets, cells with less than 250 and greater than 20,000 UMIs, less than 200 genes, and mitochondrial gene percent greater than 20% were excluded as low-quality cells. For rat retinal cell datasets, cells with counts, genes, mitochondrial gene percentage, and ribosomal gene percentage outside of three standard deviations from the mean were excluded as low-quality cells.

For hNPCs, the ‘LogNormalize’ function was used for normalization and scaling of the expression matrix for each sample, and then the ‘SelectIntegrationFeatures’ and ‘FindIntegrationAnchors’ functions were used to select the features and anchors for downstream integration. These anchor points were then used to integrate all datasets of the hNPCs through the ‘IntegrateData’ function. Next, the ‘ScaleData’ and ‘RunPCA’ functions were used for scaling and calculating principal component analysis (PCA) dimensions in the hNPC integrated datasets. Unsupervised clustering was then performed using the ‘FindNeighbors’ and ‘FindClusters’ functions, grouping the datasets into distinct clusters. Dimensionality reduction was conducted using the ‘RunUMAP’ function. Clusters were annotated based on known retinal cell type markers and hNPC-specific gene markers. Subsequently, hNPC clusters were subset and reprocessed following the same steps described above. The ‘FindAllMarkers’ and ‘FindConservedMarkers’ functions were used to identify and annotate specific markers for the hNPC clusters.

Similarly, for retinal cells, the expression matrix for each sample was normalized and scaled using the ‘SCTransform’ function91. This was followed by feature and anchor selection with the ‘PrepSCTIntegration’ and ‘FindIntegrationAnchors’ functions. The identified anchors were then used to integrate all datasets from the same tissue using the ‘IntegrateData’ function. Subsequently, the ‘ScaleData’ and ‘RunPCA’ functions were employed to scale the data and perform principal component analysis (PCA) on the integrated datasets of hNPCs and rat retinal cells. Unsupervised clustering of the datasets into distinct clusters was performed using the ‘FindNeighbors’ and ‘FindClusters’ functions. Dimensionality reduction was carried out using the ‘RunUMAP’ function. To investigate the gene expression profile of each cluster, the ‘FindAllMarkers’ function (with avg_log2FC > 0.4) was used to identify highly expressed genes (marker genes) that are specific to each cluster and correspond to distinct cell types based on marker gene expression.

Differential gene expression and functional analysis. To identify differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between in vitro and in vivo hNPCs at P60 and P90, the ‘FindMarkers’ function with the MAST92 test in Seurat was applied. DEGs between wild-type, untreated, and hNPC-treated retinal cells, across different retinal cell types, were identified using the ‘FindMarkers’ function with the Wilcoxon test. For hNPCs, we used the EnrichR93 R package (version 3.2) and the ‘gseGO’ and ‘gseKEGG’ functions from the clusterProfiler94 R package (version 4.10.1) to identify enriched biological pathways and processes in our sets of DEGs, as well as in DEGs shared across different differential expression analyses. For rat retinal cells, we employed the ‘gseGO’ and ‘gseKEGG’ functions from the clusterProfiler R package to determine enriched biological pathways and processes in our DEG sets.

Cell-cell ligand-receptor interaction analysis. We performed cell-cell ligand-receptor interaction in our scRNA-seq integrated rat retinal cell and hNPC datasets with CellChat95 (v1.6.1), using cell type labels. The human CellChatDB ligand-receptor interaction database was used for this analysis. To facilitate downstream comparisons of the signaling networks in untreated versus hNPC-treated and P60 versus P90 hNPC-treated groups, we ran the CellChat workflow separately on each dataset from different time points. The CellChat object was created using the normalized gene expression matrix and the cell type annotations, removing any cell groups with fewer than 10 cells. We then ran the recommended CellChat workflow using the following functions: identifyOverExpressedGenes, identifyOverExpressedInteractions, projectData, computeCommunProb, filterCommunication, subsetCommunication, computeCommunProbPathway, aggregateNet, and netAnalysis_computeCentrality. We separately merged P60 and P90 untreated and hNPC-treated and P60 and P90 hNPC-treated CellChat objects into one object using the mergeCellChat function. We compared the signaling networks separately at P60 and P90 between untreated and hNPC-treated groups and then between P60 and P90 hNPC-treated groups both functionally and structurally using the computeNetSimilarityPairwise function. Further, we used the rankNet function to compute the relative information flow changes between the groups across all signaling pathways. We identified differentially expressed ligands and receptors as well as their signaling pathways using the identifyOverExpressedGenes function, visualizing results with the netAnalysis_signalingRole_heatmap.

Statistics and reproducibility. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Investigators were blinded to experimental group allocation during data collection and analysis, where applicable. Single-cell RNA sequencing data were analyzed with appropriate batch correction methods. Visual function tests were performed on multiple animals per group. Histological analyses were performed at least three times to ensure reproducibility. Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Software’s PRISM (version 10), and the results are presented as the mean ± SEM. Results were analyzed by One-way ANOVA coupled with a Tukey’s multiple comparisons test for more than 2-group. For ERG and OKR, One-way ANOVA, Kruskal-Wallis test, coupled with Dunn’s Multiple comparison test were used. P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. No data were excluded from the analyses.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

The authors employed scRNA-seq to comprehensively analyze dynamic transcriptomic remodeling in grafted human neural progenitor cells. They made several key findings such as temporal gene expression changes in grafted cells and retinal cells, upregulation of novel trophic factors, cell fate of grafted cells, intercellular signaling changes, etc. The findings revealed dynamic transcriptomic changes in the degenerative retinal environment and helped our understanding of the rescue mechanism of grafted hNPCs. However, several issues need to be addressed in the paper.
Major concerns:
1. ERGs were used to assess the retinal function after hNPC treatment. However, the description of ERG results was very sketchy. It was not clear whether the ERG results were recorded under the scotopic or photopic conditions. Therefore, it was not clear how the treatments affect the rod and cone function, respectively. The authors used b-wave amplitudes to determine the rescue effect. Although b-wave amplitudes may indirectly reflect the function of photoreceptors, a-wave amplitudes should be used to gauge the function of photoreceptors, particularly rod photoreceptors.
2. Figure 4o: There was a much smaller size of con cell population in the treated retina than in the untreated retina. By contrast, the rod population in the treated retina is larger than in the untreated. Does that suggest that the hNPC treatment only protects rods but accelerates cone degeneration? If this is the case, it needs interpretation. Figure 4m has a similar trend, but less significant than in 4o, which could be due to the shorter duration of treatment. This should be reflected in the functional test results, such as ERGs.
3. Figure 5k. The heatmap shows selected 729 microglial homeostatic and activation. The comparison was made between three groups. It was not clear how the comparison was made. What was the reference expression level for each group of the sample when the upregulation or downregulation was determined?
4. In lines 362-364, gene expression profiles in Muller glia cells were compared between different groups. Downregulation of genes involved in visual 363 perception, photoreceptor cell maintenance was found. Muller glia cells are not known to express a significant amount of genes involved in visual 363 perception, photoreceptor cell maintenance. These results presented here indicate that the Muller glia cell clusters were contaminated with other photoreceptor cells. The authors should estimate whether the contamination obscured the overall conclusion.
5. Retinal degeneration in RCS rats stems from RPE malfunction. How hNPC transplantation affects the function of RPE and the contribution of gene expression profile changes in RPEs should be assessed.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Shahin et al. presents an extensive single cell transcriptomic analysis of hNPCs at two time points (P60 and P90) following placement into the subretinal space of the RCS rat model of retinal degeneration at a single time point (P21) and compares the results to untransplanted hNPCs. Emphasis was placed on DEGs related to a number of cellular processes attributed to the donor cells or the surrounding host retina. The hPSC cells of interest are currently being tested in a clinical trial, and thus they have shown sufficient promise and safety in preclinical models to warrant examining their therapeutic potential in humans.
While the effort is admirable and the results are of interest given the ongoing clinical trial, the study has numerous major limitations. More specifically, the manuscript is 1. one-dimensional with regard techniques and models (single cell transcriptomics alone with minimal immunocytochemistry and use of the RCS rat only), 2. insufficiently controlled (no sham or non-hPSC cell transplant control; no cyclosporine A-only control), 3. presented in a selectively positive manner with essentially all highlighted findings being considered a strength of the hNPC treatment, and 4. exclusively descriptive and correlative with broadly qualified conclusions without demonstration of causation – i.e., there are no direct experimental manipulations to test any of the proposed mechanisms or interactions that are speculated. Lastly, most of the findings are predictable (e.g., donor cells proliferate and then mature; host photoreceptors are preserved, which is a known effect, etc.) and do not broadly advance the field of cellular transplantation. Other comments are listed below.
1. The RCS rat has a known sham effect with photoreceptor survival occurring with any subretinal intervention. A sham control and a non hNPC cell transplant control is needed to show specific effects of hNPCs.
2. No evaluation of the RPE is provided, and the RCS rat harbors a primary mutation in the RPE cells with a secondary effect on photoreceptors. How does the transplant affect the health of the host RPE?
3. All of the single cell transcriptomic analyses are broadly presented and speculated to have causal relationships when no such conclusions can be drawn from the studies presented.
4. The ICC shown suggests that the majority of transplanted cells do not integrate in the host retina (contrary to the comments in the introduction that state that they migrate extensively within the host retina). Instead, they stay mostly as a mass between the RPE and retina. No effort to discern the fate of cells within the host retina or adjacent to it is provided.
5. Cells were delivered only at one timepoint in the RCS rat – assuming that patients will be treated at different stages of their disease, results obtained from an injection at only one early time point significantly reduces the impact of the results.
6. The rats were immunosuppressed with cyclosporine A but there was no control provided for the effect of this drug alone (in the absence of cell transplantation).

### Reviewer 3

This study unveils the dynamic transcriptomic changes of grafted stem cells within the host’s degenerative environment over time, which fill in the knowledge gap in regenerative medicine. The findings will have broad implications for the field of stem cell therapy for degenerative diseases such as Parkson’s disease and ALS. Furthermore the study strongly suggests that both engineering stem cells with additional trophic factor(s) such as MANF for modulating microglia and Muller glia, and improving host’s degenerative environment are essential for ensuring long-term efficacy in regenerative medicine. In summary, stem cells and trophic factors as add-onto improve host environment are needed for long-term vision protection.
Overall, the design is sound, experimental data are interesting and conclusions are well supported.
I have some minor concerns.
1.This study only covered two time points (P60 and P90), early and later time points are needed to capture the temporal dynamics of grafted hNPC and host retinal changes.
2.Injection at P21, early time of retinal degeneration, later time points of grafting should be performed.
3.It would be interesting to present additional study using hNPCengineered to release trophic factor MANF to see whether the therapeutic effect will be enhanced; how hNPC-MANF modulates host retinal environment.
4.The graft-associated effect on host photoreceptors, Muller glia and microglia is estimated since we cannot dissect precisely grafted-related area. Spatial transcriptomics would be ideal to address directly host retinal cells affected by graft.

## Authors' Response to Round 1

We are very grateful for reviewers’ thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below, we provide point-to-point responses to each concern, outlining the steps we have taken to strengthen the study and clarify its scope:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors employed scRNA-seq to comprehensively analyze dynamic transcriptomic remodeling in grafted human neural progenitor cells. They made several key findings such as temporal gene expression changes in grafted cells and retinal cells, upregulation of novel trophic factors, cell fate of grafted cells, intercellular signaling changes, etc. The findings revealed dynamic transcriptomic changes in the degenerative retinal environment and helped our understanding of the rescue mechanism of grafted hNPCs. However, several issues need to be addressed in the paper.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful summary and constructive feedback. To our knowledge, this is the first study to comprehensively characterize the dynamic transcriptomic remodeling of both grafted human neural progenitor cells (hNPCs) and the host retinal cells over time in a degenerative environment. Our findings demonstrate that the efficacy of a single stem cell-based therapy may decline as retinal degeneration progresses. This highlights the need for a combinatorial therapeutic strategy, integrating stem cell transplantation with interventions targeting the degenerative host retinal environment to achieve sustained vision preservation.
Major concerns:
1. ERGs were used to assess the retinal function after hNPC treatment. However, the description of ERG results was very sketchy. It was not clear whether the ERG results were recorded under the scotopic or photopic conditions. Therefore, it was not clear how the treatments affect the rod and cone function, respectively. The authors used b-wave amplitudes to determine the rescue effect. Although b-wave amplitudes may indirectly reflect the function of photoreceptors, a-wave amplitudes should be used to gauge the function of photoreceptors, particularly rod photoreceptors.
Response: Thank you for this insightful and critical comment. We fully agree that clarifying the ERG methodology and distinguishing between rod and cone function is important for interpreting ERG data. In the RCS rat model, rod photoreceptor function declines rapidly and is compromised by postnatal day (P) 21, leaving cones as the primary contributors to residual/remaining retinal function. Our prior studies have consistently demonstrated that while stem cell therapy does not restore lost rod function, it can preserve cone-mediated responses (e.g., Girman et al. 2005, PMID: 15607350; Lu et al. 2023, PMID: 37743503; Shahin et al. 2023, PMID: 37786347).
We have revised the manuscript to clarify the ERG recording conditions in the Method section under the heading Electroretinography (ERG) and interpretation in the Results section:
Method section (lines 931-936): "In brief, following overnight (14-16h) dark adaptation, animals were prepared under dim red light. Scotopic ERGs were recorded by stimulating the eyes with 5 ms white-light flashes at an intensity of 25 cd/m² with 10 s interstimulus intervals using a computer-controlled Espion system (Diagnosys LLC). A total of 20-30 sweeps were recorded for each animal, and the averaged responses were used to determine the response amplitude and assess rod-mediated retinal function.”
Results section (lines 120-131): "After overnight dark adaptation, animals were prepared under dim red light. Scotopic ERGs were recorded using 5 ms white-light flashes at 25 cd/m² with 10-second interstimulus intervals, to assess rod-mediated retinal function. As expected, a-waves were not detectable at P60 and P90, due to loss of rod photoreceptor outer segment activity, which is known to be compromised as early as P21 in the RCS model, as reported in our previous study17. However, ERG b-wave amplitudes were significantly higher for hNPC-treated eyes compared to untreated controls at P60 and P90 (Supplementary Fig.1c). These b-wave responses are primarily cone-driven, demonstrating preservation of inner retinal activity, consistent with our previous findings15,17. Notably, while visual acuity (tested under photopic condition) for hNPC-treated eyes was significantly higher than untreated controls and remained stable, ERG b-wave amplitudes decreased over time, reflecting progressive deterioration of retinal function (Supplementary Fig.1b-c)."
We acknowledge the reviewer's point that a-wave amplitudes most directly reflect photoreceptor (particularly rod) function. However, due to the early rod degeneration in RCS rats, a-wave measurements provide negligible functional information at later stages, such as P60 and P90 time points in our study. Our focus on b-wave amplitudes is therefore justified and aligns with established methodology in this RP model. The scotopic b-wave in the RCS rat reflects the activity of inner retinal cells (bipolar and Müller cells) that remain responsive to surviving photoreceptor input.
2. Figure 4o: There was a much smaller size of con cell population in the treated retina than in the untreated retina. By contrast, the rod population in the treated retina is larger than in the untreated. Does that suggest that the hNPC treatment only protects rods but accelerates cone degeneration? If this is the case, it needs interpretation. Figure 4m has a similar trend, but less significant than in 4o, which could be due to the shorter duration of treatment. This should be reflected in the functional test results, such as ERGs.
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful comment. We emphasize that hNPC treatment protects both rods and cones, as demonstrated in our previous studies (Wang et al. 2011, PMID: 18579765; Lu et al. 2023, PMID: 37743503; Shahin et al. 2023, PMID: 37786347). To strengthen this conclusion, we incorporated new supporting data (new Supplementary Fig. 2) confirming photoreceptor protection. Specifically, recoverin immunostaining, which labels both rods and cones, revealed a preserved outer nuclear layer in the graft-protected areas, whereas only a single layer of photoreceptors remained in the untreated retina. Cone-arrestin staining further confirmed well-organized cones with inner and outer segments in regions associated with hNPC-grafted area. In contrast, age-matched untreated retinas displayed degenerative cone morphology with diminished cone-arrestin signals. These histological findings are consistent with functional outcomes. ERG recordings demonstrated significantly higher b-wave amplitudes in hNPC-treated eyes compared to untreated controls, reflecting preserved cone-driven retinal responses. Together, these data confirm that hNPCs protect both rod and cone photoreceptors.
We have incorporated all these findings in the result section of the revised manuscript (lines 133-153).
The apparent reduction in cone numbers in Fig. 4o is likely due to sampling variability rather than real cone loss. This is further supported by cone-arrestin staining and ERG results, which demonstrate clear preservation of cone structure and function in treated retinas.
3. Figure 5k. The heatmap shows selected 729 microglial homeostatic and activation. The comparison was made between three groups. It was not clear how the comparison was made. What was the reference expression level for each group of the sample when the upregulation or downregulation was determined?
Response: Thank you for pointing out the need for clarification. In Fig. 5k, each row (i.e., each gene) was z–score normalized across the three experimental groups at a given time point (WT, Untreated, and hNPC-Treated). Specifically, at P60 (and likewise at P90), we first calculated the pseudo-bulk average expression of each gene within each group. We then computed the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of these three values, and derived the z-score for each group i as:

where E is the average expression of the gene in group i. Thus, the “reference” is the mean expression of that gene across all three groups at the corresponding time point. Positive z-scores (reddish) indicate expression above the overall mean, whereas negative z-scores (bluish) indicate expression below it. This normalization enables direct pattern comparison across groups while controlling for baseline differences.
4. In lines 362-364, gene expression profiles in Muller glia cells were compared between different groups. Downregulation of genes involved in visual 363 perception, photoreceptor cell maintenance was found. Muller glia cells are not known to express a significant amount of genes involved in visual 363 perception, photoreceptor cell maintenance. These results presented here indicate that the Muller glia cell clusters were contaminated with other photoreceptor cells. The authors should estimate whether the contamination obscured the overall conclusion.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that under physiological conditions, Müller glia are not major contributors to pathways involved in visual perception or photoreceptor maintenance. However, in the context of retinal degeneration, Müller glia are known to upregulate genes typically associated with photoreceptors as part of a reactive or compensatory program (Tomita et al., 2021, PMID: 34799683).
To address this, we have clarified the manuscript (lines 431-435): “Of note, Müller glia upregulate genes involved in phototransduction and light stimulus in response to retinal degeneration. However, in hNPC-treated Müller glia, downregulation of genes related to these biological processes suggests that hNPCs may modulate Müller glia reactivity, shifting their transcriptional profile away from compensatory photoreceptor-like responses and toward a supportive, neuroprotective state.”
Importantly, we carefully re-examined the clustering and marker gene expression profiles and found no evidence of photoreceptor contamination within the Müller glia clusters. The cell identities remain consistent with established Müller glial markers, and the overall conclusions are robust to this analysis. We are therefore confident that the observed changes represent genuine Müller glial responses to hNPC treatment rather than artifacts of misclassification or contamination.
5. Retinal degeneration in RCS rats stems from RPE malfunction. How hNPC transplantation affects the function of RPE and the contribution of gene expression profile changes in RPEs should be assessed.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point. In our study, we observed that RPE cell integrity, as indicated by RPE65 and collagen IV immunostaining, was preserved in regions associated with grafted hNPC distribution (new Supplementary Fig. 2 and new Fig. 8). Additionally, we did not observe the characteristic subretinal debris accumulation typically seen in RCS rats, which results from RPE dysfunction and failure to phagocytose photoreceptor outer segments (OS), as previously reported (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165, Shahin et al. 2023, PMID: 37786347). Both our current and prior studies demonstrate that grafted hNPCs are capable of phagocytosing OS, thereby compensating for the defective RPE and helping to maintain a healthy subretinal environment.
While we did not directly assess RPE transcriptomes, the preserved RPE morphology, absence of subretinal debris, and evidence of hNPC-mediated phagocytosis together suggest that hNPCs indirectly support RPE function, which likely contributes to the observed photoreceptor protection.
In this study, we did not isolate RPE cells for transcriptomic analysis, as our primary goal was to recover grafted hNPCs and retinal cells (especially photoreceptors and glial cells) from a large number of eyes while preserving RNA quality. We agree with the reviewer that future studies focusing on RPE-specific gene expression changes in response to hNPC transplantation will be important to further elucidate their contribution to therapeutic efficacy.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Shahin et al. presents an extensive single cell transcriptomic analysis of hNPCs at two time points (P60 and P90) following placement into the subretinal space of the RCS rat model of retinal degeneration at a single time point (P21) and compares the results to untransplanted hNPCs. Emphasis was placed on DEGs related to a number of cellular processes attributed to the donor cells or the surrounding host retina. The hPSC cells of interest are currently being tested in a clinical trial, and thus they have shown sufficient promise and safety in preclinical models to warrant examining their therapeutic potential in humans.
While the effort is admirable and the results are of interest given the ongoing clinical trial, the study has numerous major limitations. More specifically, the manuscript is 1. one-dimensional with regard techniques and models (single cell transcriptomics alone with minimal immunocytochemistry and use of the RCS rat only), 2. insufficiently controlled (no sham or non-hPSC cell transplant control; no cyclosporine A-only control), 3. presented in a selectively positive manner with essentially all highlighted findings being considered a strength of the hNPC treatment, and 4. exclusively descriptive and correlative with broadly qualified conclusions without demonstration of causation – i.e., there are no direct experimental manipulations to test any of the proposed mechanisms or interactions that are speculated. Lastly, most of the findings are predictable (e.g., donor cells proliferate and then mature; host photoreceptors are preserved, which is a known effect, etc.) and do not broadly advance the field of cellular transplantation. Other comments are listed below.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these critical and constructive comments. We recognize the importance of addressing these limitations directly and have revised the manuscript accordingly. Below, we provide point to point responses to each concern, outlining the steps we have taken to strengthen the study and clarify its scope:
1. One-dimensional with regard techniques and models (single cell transcriptomics alone with minimal immunocytochemistry and use of the RCS rat only).
Response: We acknowledge the reviewer’s concern regarding the scope of study. Our decision to focus on the well-characterized RCS rat model was deliberate, as it allowed us to build directly upon our previous IND-enabling study (Lu et al. 2023, PMID: 37743503). While we agree that future investigations comparing grafted hNPC behavior across multiple retinal degeneration models would provide valuable insights, the depth of our single-cell transcriptomic analysis in this highly relevant model offers a unique and unprecedented view of the dynamic cellular interactions between grafted hNPCs and the host retina. Furthermore, our previously published work has already demonstrated the limited proliferation of grafted hNPCs (Shahin et al. 2023, PMID: 37786347; Lu et al. 2023, PMID: 37743503), which is a key safety feature emphasized by the FDA.
We also fully agree that validation of key transcriptomic findings at the protein level is essential. To address this, we have significantly revised our manuscript by performing extensive new immunohistochemistry analyses and incorporating five new figures. These additional analyses strengthen and validate our key scRNA-seq findings at the protein level. Below, we outline the steps we have taken to strengthen the study and clarify its scope.
Fig.1i: Characterization of grafted hNPCs at the protein level
Our transcriptomic data suggested that grafted hNPCs predominantly adopt a glial-like fate. This finding is now confirmed by immunofluorescence staining, which demonstrates robust expression of the astrocytic markers GFAP and AQP4. Grafted hNPCs also retained key neural progenitor markers like Nestin and SOX2. We observed only a few OLIG2- and DCX-positive cells, which precisely corroborates the low abundance of OPC-like and neuronal populations identified in our scRNA-seq dataset.
Findings are incorporated in the results section of the revised manuscript (lines 203-213).
Supplementary Fig. 2: Protection of photoreceptors and RPE integrity by hNPCs
We have incorporated histological evidence demonstrating that grafted hNPCs preserved both rod and cone photoreceptors as well as RPE integrity. Recoverin staining confirmed preservation of both photoreceptor types in areas corresponding to hNPC grafts, whereas untreated controls showed only a single remaining photoreceptor layer. Cone-arrestin staining revealed well-organized cones with intact inner and outer segments in graft-associated regions, in contrast to the degenerative cone morphology and diminished staining seen in untreated controls. Additionally, RPE65 and Collagen IV staining confirmed RPE preservation in hNPC-treated areas, while both markers were weak or absent in untreated retinas.
Findings are incorporated in the results section of the revised manuscript (lines 133-153).
Supplementary Fig. 10: Validation of RdCVF (Nxnl1/Txnl6) expression in the RCS retina following hNPC treatment
hNPC-treated retinas showed increased expression of Txnl6 (Nxnl1), compared to untreated controls. However, P90 hNPC-treated retinas exhibited reduced Txnl6 (Nxnl1) expression compared to P60 hNPC-treated retinas.
Fig. 8: Expression of Extracellular Matrix Molecules
Our scRNA-seq data indicated that grafted hNPCs express extracellular matrix (ECM) molecules involved in supportive functions. We have now validated this finding at the protein level, demonstrating that grafted hNPCs express ECM molecules such as Tenascin-C. In addition, we also show that grafted hNPCs preserve host retinal ECM integrity by maintaining the levels of collagen IV and IMPG2, which provide support to RPE cells and maintain the structural stability of the photoreceptor outer segment.
Findings are incorporated in the results section of the revised manuscript (lines 550-555).
Supplementary Fig. 14g-h: Validation of NCAM signaling
Our scRNA-seq data indicated that grafted hNPCs upregulate cell adhesion molecule (CAM) signaling, including NCAM1, which contributes to synaptic stability and visual signal transmission. We now validated this finding at the protein level, demonstrating increased NCAM1 expression in both grafted hNPCs and the host retina at P60 compared to P90.
Findings are incorporated in the results section of the revised manuscript (lines 541-543).
Together, we believe, these additions significantly broaden the scope of our study by providing complementary protein-level validation, while preserving the unique depth of insight offered by scRNA-seq.
2. insufficiently controlled (no sham or non-hPSC cell transplant control; no cyclosporine A-only control).
Response: We included untreated (non-hNPC transplant) control groups at both P60 and P90 time points for comparison. All experimental animals, including controls, received cyclosporine A in their drinking water following our previously established protocols (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165; Lu et al. 2015, PMID: 25694843), as cyclosporine A has been reported to influence visual function in the RCS rat model (Cooper et al. 2016, PMID: 27008099). Our design thus ensured that any observed differences were attributable to the presence or absence of hNPC transplantation rather than the effects of immunosuppression alone.
Our study was designed to examine the biological impact of grafted hNPCs and their interactions with the host retina, rather than to evaluate the surgical procedure itself. As such, we did not include a sham-operated group (surgery without cell delivery), since our focus was not on isolating the effects of the surgical intervention. We acknowledge that inclusion of sham or non-hPSC cell transplant controls will be an important consideration in proof-of-concept study. Our previously published studies, which included sham-operated and non-hPSC cell transplant controls, demonstrated that the surgical procedure alone does not provide the therapeutic effects observed with hNPCs (Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347; Lu et al., 2023, PMID: 37743503). Based on these foundational findings, we focused the present study on a direct comparison between hNPC-treated and untreated retinas to specifically address the molecular mechanisms underlying the therapeutic benefits of the hNPCs themselves.
3. presented in a selectively positive manner with essentially all highlighted findings being considered a strength of the hNPC treatment
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We fully agree that it is important to present both the strengths and limitations of hNPC treatment transparently for a balanced and rigorous interpretation of our findings. In the revised manuscript, we have clarified that hNPC transplantation does not halt retinal degeneration but rather slows disease progression. For example, we explicitly note that while ERG b-wave amplitudes remain significantly higher in hNPC-treated eyes compared to controls, they still decline over time, and some photoreceptor loss continues by P90. This reflects a slowing, rather than a complete prevention of degenerative processes.
We also expanded the Limitations section to emphasize the descriptive and hypothesis-generating nature of our single-cell and CellChat analyses. We acknowledged that further functional studies are required to establish causality for the pathways identified. These revisions ensure that while we highlight the meaningful neuroprotective role of hNPCs, our presentation remains scientifically balanced, reinforcing the idea that this approach is a valuable component of a broader therapeutic strategy to modify the degenerative retinal environment.
4. exclusively descriptive and correlative with broadly qualified conclusions without demonstration of causation – i.e., there are no direct experimental manipulations to test any of the proposed mechanisms or interactions that are speculated.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. This study was designed as a descriptive and hypothesis-generating investigation, and we acknowledge that no direct experimental manipulations were performed to establish causation for the proposed mechanisms and interactions. Retinal degenerative disease is a highly complicated process involving dynamic remodeling of multiple cell types, and our goal was to capture these temporal transcriptomic changes, understand how grafted hNPCs evolve in a progressive degenerative environment, and identify potential therapeutic targets to enhance hNPC therapeutic efficacy. Our findings highlight several promising avenues for intervention, including engineering hNPCs to overexpress trophic factors such as MANF and targeting key retinal support cells such as Müller glia and microglia, as adjunctive strategies to enhance photoreceptor survival. These targets will be systematically validated in follow-up studies using genetic and pharmacological approaches.
5. Lastly, most of the findings are predictable (e.g., donor cells proliferate and then mature; host photoreceptors are preserved, which is a known effect, etc.) and do not broadly advance the field of cellular transplantation.
Response: We respectfully disagree with the suggestion that the findings are predictable or lack broader significance. First, our data, consistent with previous reports from our group (Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347; Lu et al., 2023, PMID: 37743503) demonstrate that grafted hNPCs exhibit minimal or no proliferation after transplantation. This limited proliferative capacity is not only non-trivial but also critically important from a translational and regulatory standpoint, as non-proliferation is a key safety requirement outlined by the FDA for cell-based therapies.
While photoreceptor preservation has been observed in earlier studies involving stem cell transplantation, the mechanisms underlying this protective effect remain poorly understood. Our study is, to our knowledge, the first to systematically examine both graft and host retinal transcriptomic remodeling over time, revealing that stem cell therapy initiates a dynamic and bidirectional molecular cross-talk between transplanted cells and the degenerating retina.
Importantly, our findings show that:
• A single delivery of stem cells may not have long-last effects on vision preservation.
• Long-term neuroprotection requires addressing the degenerative host microenvironment, especially by modulating key retinal support cells such as Müller glia and microglia.
• These insights not only refine the understanding of stem cell behavior in the retina but also have broader implications for regenerative medicine strategies targeting other neurodegenerative diseases, such as Parkinson’s disease and ALS, where glial and degenerative host environment significantly influence therapeutic outcomes.
Thus, our study moves beyond simply documenting known outcomes and instead provides a conceptual framework and actionable insights for improving stem cell–based therapies in retinal and CNS degenerative diseases.
Other comments’ responses are listed below.
1. The RCS rat has a known sham effect with photoreceptor survival occurring with any subretinal intervention. A sham control and a non hNPC cell transplant control is needed to show specific effects of hNPCs.
Response: We agree with the reviewer that the RCS rat exhibits a well-documented sham effect, where short-term photoreceptor preservation can occur following subretinal intervention, independent of the transplanted cell type. In our previous studies (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165; Lu et al. 2015, PMID: 25694843; Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347; Lu et al., 2023, PMID: 37743503), we directly addressed this issue by including sham-operated and untreated control groups, which clearly demonstrated the specific therapeutic effects of hNPCs beyond the sham response. These data formed the foundation for the ongoing clinical trial.
The current study builds on that body of work by shifting focus toward understanding the temporal dynamics of grafted hNPCs and their molecular interactions with host retinal cells. Our goal was not to re-demonstrate efficacy over sham but rather to explore how both graft and host undergo transcriptomic and cellular remodeling over time. These insights provide a mechanistic understanding of the limitations of single-dose therapy and point to new opportunities to enhance long-term efficacy through modulation of the host retinal environment.
2. No evaluation of the RPE is provided, and the RCS rat harbors a primary mutation in the RPE cells with a secondary effect on photoreceptors. How does the transplant affect the health of the host RPE?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the importance of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) in the RCS rat model, which indeed carries a primary mutation in Mertk that impairs RPE phagocytosis, leading to secondary photoreceptor degeneration.
In the current study, we evaluated RPE integrity using RPE65 and Collagen IV immunostaining, which showed preserved RPE structure in regions associated with grafted hNPCs (new Supplementary Fig. 2 and new Fig. 8). These findings are consistent with our previous studies (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165; Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347) showing reduced subretinal debris accumulation in hNPC-protected areas. In the RCS model, undigested outer segments (OS) accumulate in the subretinal space due to defective RPE phagocytosis. Our data support that grafted hNPCs can compensate for this dysfunction by directly phagocytosing OS (Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347), thereby helping to maintain a healthier subretinal environment.
While we did not isolate host RPE cells for transcriptomic analysis in this study, due to our emphasis on recovering high-quality RNA from grafted hNPCs and host retinal cells across a large number of eyes, we agree that a focused evaluation of RPE-specific gene expression changes in response to hNPC transplantation would provide important mechanistic insight. We plan to pursue this in future studies using targeted approaches such as RPE-specific single-cell transcriptomics.
3. All of the single cell transcriptomic analyses are broadly presented and speculated to have causal relationships when no such conclusions can be drawn from the studies presented.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important point. Below we clarify how our manuscript frames all single‐cell and CellChat analyses as correlative and hypothesis‐generating, and we highlight our language choices and explicit “Limitations” statements that underscore the need for functional validation.
1. Observational Nature of scRNA-seq and CellChat Analyses
• Throughout the Results (e.g., lines: 102–113), we describe dynamic shifts in gene expression, such as upregulation of MANF, MDK, PTN, MYDGF, and their receptors in grafted hNPCs, and declines in intercellular communication strength over time. These sections present fold-changes and pathway enrichments but do not claim causation.
• Similarly, our CellChat analyses (Fig. 7, lines: 504–555) identify changes in ligand–receptor “communication probability” and “information flow,” which we characterize as predictive network inferences rather than demonstrations of functional effect.
2. Careful Language in Discussion
In the Discussion, we consistently use verbs such as suggest, indicate, and highlight the potential when referring to identified pathways (lines: 576–587), thereby framing these as hypotheses to be tested, not proven causal mechanisms. For eg.,
“These findings suggest that enhancing trophic factor support, particularly MANF, … are critical for sustaining long-term vision preservation.”
Here, “suggest” explicitly signals that follow-up studies are required.
3. Explicit Limitations and Call for Functional Follow-Up
We dedicate a section, “Limitations of the study” (lines: 654–665) to acknowledge that our work is descriptive and that functional perturbation experiments (e.g., genetic manipulation of therapeutic targets, time-course intervention) are needed to establish causality.
Text excerpt:
“While this study provides valuable insights into the transcriptomic remodeling of grafted hNPCs and host retinal cells over time, additional later time points and loss- or gain-of-function experiments will be required to test the precise mechanistic roles of identified trophic factors and signaling pathways.”
In summary, we fully acknowledge that our single-cell and CellChat data are correlative and presented as such. We have used precise, hypothesis-generating terminology throughout and explicitly state the need for functional validation in our Limitations section. We trust this clarification fully addresses the reviewer’s concern.
4. The ICC shown suggests that the majority of transplanted cells do not integrate in the host retina (contrary to the comments in the introduction that state that they migrate extensively within the host retina). Instead, they stay mostly as a mass between the RPE and retina. No effort to discern the fate of cells within the host retina or adjacent to it is provided.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments. Our findings indicate that the majority of grafted hNPCs did not integrate into the host retina but rather remained in the subretinal space, where they adopted a glial-like fate. As demonstrated in our previously published studies (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165; Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347; Lu et al., 2023, PMID: 37743503), these cells are distributed in two forms in the subretinal space: a lump of cells near the injection site or in the form of a continuous line (2-3 layers) within the subretinal space between the RPE and photoreceptors (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165; Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347; Lu et al., 2023, PMID: 37743503). In our revised manuscript, we have now added images (new Fig. 1i) showing the characterization and migratory distribution of hNPCs in the subretinal space.
5. Cells were delivered only at one timepoint in the RCS rat – assuming that patients will be treated at different stages of their disease, results obtained from an injection at only one early time point significantly reduces the impact of the results.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s important observation. Indeed, most preclinical studies, including ours, have historically initiated cell transplantation at early stages of disease progression to maximize the opportunity for preservation of retinal structure and function. However, as the reviewer correctly points out, patients typically present at varying stages of retinal degeneration, and it is essential to understand how disease stage influences treatment efficacy.
We recognize this limitation and have explicitly stated it in the limitation of the study. Importantly, in our previous studies, we have evaluated the efficacy of different cell types, including hNPCs, when delivered at mid or late stages of retinal degeneration (Wang et al. 2011, PMID: 18579765; Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347), showing stage-dependent differences in treatment outcomes.
The current study was specifically designed to examine temporal molecular and cellular changes following hNPC transplantation, and thus focused on a single, early time point for delivery to ensure consistent analysis of graft–host interactions over time. Moving forward, we fully agree that it will be critical to extend this approach to include cell transplantation at multiple disease stages, in order to better reflect clinical reality and optimize therapeutic strategies for patients at different stages along the degenerative spectrum.
6. The rats were immunosuppressed with cyclosporine A but there was no control provided for the effect of this drug alone (in the absence of cell transplantation).
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to the study design. However, we respectfully note that the primary objective of this study was to investigate the biological interactions between grafted hNPCs and the host retina, particularly the dynamic transcriptomic changes occurring over time. To achieve this, it was necessary to maintain immune compatibility and minimize graft rejection by administering Cyclosporine A (CsA) to all animals that received hNPCs, consistent with our previous protocols (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165; Lu et al. 2015, PMID: 25694843).
While we recognize that cyclosporine A can have biological effects on its own, we designed the study such that all animals, both transplanted and untreated controls received identical immunosuppression, allowing us to isolate the impact of hNPC transplantation. Given that our aim was to investigate dynamic transcriptomic changes and interaction between grafted hNPCs and the host retina, a CsA-only group would not have provided additional mechanistic insight into the questions we sought to address. Nevertheless, we agree that the independent effects of immunosuppression could be an interesting focus for future studies.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This study unveils the dynamic transcriptomic changes of grafted stem cells within the host’s degenerative environment over time, which fill in the knowledge gap in regenerative medicine. The findings will have broad implications for the field of stem cell therapy for degenerative diseases such as Parkson’s disease and ALS. Furthermore the study strongly suggests that both engineering stem cells with additional trophic factor(s) such as MANF for modulating microglia and Muller glia, and improving host’s degenerative environment are essential for ensuring long-term efficacy in regenerative medicine. In summary, stem cells and trophic factors as add-on to improve host environment are needed for long-term vision protection.
Overall, the design is sound, experimental data are interesting and conclusions are well supported.
Response: Thank you very much for your positive and encouraging comments. We agree that the dynamic transcriptomic insights provided by this study fill an important knowledge gap in regenerative medicine. We also believe that our findings have broad implications beyond retinal degeneration, potentially informing stem cell therapies for neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease and ALS. We appreciate your recognition of the study design and data, and we look forward to further advancing this field by exploring strategies to optimize both graft function and the host environment for long-term therapeutic benefit.
I have some minor concerns.
1.This study only covered two time points (P60 and P90), early and later time points are needed to capture the temporal dynamics of grafted hNPC and host retinal changes.
Response: We completely agree with the reviewer’s point. Expanding the analysis to include additional early and later time points will be critical to fully capture the temporal dynamics of grafted hNPCs and host retinal responses. Our selection of P60 and P90 was deliberate. This allowed us to focus on two key phases of retinal degeneration in the RCS rat model: P60, a time point when photoreceptor degeneration is well-established but not complete, and P90, a later stage of severe degeneration. This provided a focused snapshot of the hNPC-mediated molecular and cellular changes during the critical intermediate and late phases of disease progression.
We plan to incorporate such comprehensive longitudinal studies in future work to further elucidate the progression of graft–host interactions over time.
2.Injection at P21, early time of retinal degeneration, later time points of grafting should be performed.
Response: Thank you for raising this important question. We agree that the timing of cell transplantation is a critical factor, as patients present at the clinic with different stages of retinal degeneration. In our previous studies, we have shown encouraging results following cell transplantation at later stages of retinal degeneration (Wang et al. 2011, PMID: 18579765; Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347). The current study was specifically designed to provide a detailed and foundational understanding of the temporal dynamics of grafted hNPCs and their interactions with the host retina. To achieve this, we performed a comprehensive time-course analysis from a single, well-defined starting point. We fully agree with the reviewer that capturing the dynamic changes of grafted stem cells and host retina at later time points will be more directly relevant to the clinical setting, and we plan to pursue this in future studies.
3.It would be interesting to present additional study using hNPC engineered to release trophic factor MANF to see whether the therapeutic effect will be enhanced; how hNPC-MANF modulates host retinal environment.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful suggestion. Our previous studies have demonstrated that hNPCs engineered to express GDNF provide enhanced vision protection (Gamm et al. 2007, PMID: 17396165; Shahin et al, 2023, PMID: 37786347). We have also successfully engineered hNPCs to express MANF, and other trophic factors, and ongoing studies in our laboratory are currently investigating how hNPC-MANF modulates the host retinal environment and whether it can further improve therapeutic outcomes. We look forward to reporting these results in the near future.
4.The graft-associated effect on host photoreceptors, Muller glia and microglia is estimated since we cannot dissect precisely grafted-related area. Spatial transcriptomics would be ideal to address directly host retinal cells affected by graft.
Response: Thank you for this insightful comment. We fully acknowledge that the retinal dissections inevitably encompass both graft-adjacent and more distal host regions, limiting the ability to localize transcriptomic changes exclusively to cells in direct proximity to the graft.
We agree that spatial transcriptomics represents the ideal approach to directly map host retinal cells affected by hNPC grafts and to delineate the microenvironmental interactions driving these changes. While such technology was not available at our institute during the execution of this study, we view it as an essential next step and are actively pursuing its integration in follow-up work.
Importantly, despite this limitation, our combined scRNA-seq and CellChat analyses captured consistent and biologically meaningful remodeling of Müller glia, microglia, and photoreceptors in hNPC-treated retinas. These findings provide strong evidence that grafting alters host retinal cell states and intercellular communication, establishing a valuable foundation upon which future spatially resolved studies can build to more precisely define graft–host dynamics.
reviewer_updating.target:
### Reviewer 1

The authors have addressed most of the concerns. The question regarding ERGs persists. The previous report showed that the a-wave amplitude of scotopic for RCS rats at P21 was normal (Sauve Y et al., PMID: 14599567), contrasted to what was described by the authors in the revised manuscript. The a wave was pretty evident in P51 treated animals, although absent from untreated. The reason that the authors did not observe a wave in their P60 treated animals is probably due to the inappropriate condition used for recordings. Under the condition (25 cd·s/m², 10 s interval, and up to 30 traces for the scotopic ERGs) described in the paper, rods could have been bleached and become light-adapted, leaving only cone-driven responses, but not rod responses out there. Therefore, the ERG data shown in the paper only indicate preservation of cone function. To obtain rod ERG signals, it is recommended the interval is increased to 2 min and traces reduced to one or two if 25 cd·s/m² is used.
Minor point:
1. The unit for light intensity is cd·s/m², rather than cd/m².

### Reviewer 2

In this revision, the authors acknowledge some of the limitations of the study – most notably that it is purely descriptive. They also added some IHC to the manuscript, confirming the identity of cell types within the graft (primarily astrocytes) and expression of a few of the transcripts identified by sc-RNAseq analysis. No other changes or additions of significance are apparent. As such, this reviewer's prior comments largely remain.
It remains to be seen if any of the effects of these specific donor cells on host photoreceptor preservation in the RCS rat would extend to other animal models. In this manuscript, there is a lot of theorizing about how changes in the expression of specific genes by scRNA-seq may have led to preservation of host photoreceptors. However, as previously mentioned, no experimental manipulations were performed to evaluate these theories (for example, knocking down any of the identified upregulated growth factors). As such, no underlying mechanisms have been determined, and it remains to be seen if changes in any specific genes were directly responsible for host photoreceptor preservation. As this is a purely descriptive paper and not mechanistic, I suggest removal of all of the mechanistic theorizing from the results section, and just simply describe the gene expression changes (that is, all of the speculation should go in the discussion). As it currently is written a large portion of the results section reads like a discussion section. Some examples are below:
235-239: “Increased expression of MANF, MYDGF, and their receptors in grafted hNPCs at P90 compared to P60, suggest their autocrine neuroprotection to hNPCs, supporting their self-protection, stability, and survival in the progressive degenerative retinal environment. Moreover, increased secretory MANF and MYDGF, alongside their autocrine protection to hNPCs, may also protect photoreceptors via KDELR through paracrine action.”
247-252: “Altogether, these findings suggest that MDK and PTN promote grafted hNPC migration and survival through their autocrine and paracrine action, while MANF and MYDGF promote grafted hNPC survival and function via inhibiting cellular oxidative stress, inflammation, and immune response as degeneration progresses. Given their critical roles in hNPC stability and neuroprotection, these trophic factors could serve as therapeutic targets to enhance the efficacy of hNPC-based therapies for retinal degenerative diseases.”
And lastly, from new text incorporated into the revision:
430-434: “Of note, Müller glia upregulate genes involved in phototransduction and light stimulus in response to retinal degeneration. However, in hNPC-treated Müller glia, downregulation of genes related to these biological processes suggests that hNPCs may modulate Müller glia reactivity, shifting their transcriptional profile away from compensatory photoreceptor-like responses and toward a supportive, neuroprotective state.”
This new text exemplifies the point of data overinterpretation. This is just one of many potential theories that could explain the changes in the host Muller glia gene expression profile (one should also rule out the presence of photoreceptor transcripts in Muller glia as a result of phagocytosis in the non-transplanted degenerate retina).
Lastly, throughout the manuscript, preservation of host photoreceptors is attributed to gene expression changes in the transplanted cells or changes in gene expression patterns in the host retina (as a direct result of the transplanted cells). However, no direct evidence is provided to support these theories. At the end of the day, it could very well be that any donor cell type in the RCS subretinal space (or any sort of physical separation of the RPE from the neural retina in this model) would/could lead to a preservation of host PRs. These and other plausible, nonspecific mechanistic explanations need to be included in the interpretation of the data. The inclusion of such alternative explanations is especially important in the continued absence of a sham surgery control.

### Reviewer 3

all my concerns have been satisfactorily addressed.

## Paper

## Abstract

Human neural progenitor cells (hNPCs) show promise in slowing retinal degeneration and are currently being tested in clinical trials for retinitis pigmentosa (RP). However, the long-term fate of grafted hNPCs and their interaction with host retinal cells remain unclear. Here, we used single-cell transcriptomics to investigate temporal gene expression changes in grafted hNPCs and host retinal cells following subretinal injection into a rodent model of RP, revealing dynamic transcriptomic changes in the degenerative retinal environment. Grafted hNPCs primarily differentiate into an astroglial phenotype and mature over time, contributing to photoreceptor protection through trophic factor secretion, metabolic modulation, suppression of apoptosis, oxidative stress, and inflammation, alongside extracellular matrix remodeling. CellChat analysis revealed a decline in intercellular signaling and communication strength over time, correlating with weakened hNPC-host interactions. These findings suggest that enhancing trophic factor support, particularly MANF, and improving the host retinal environment are critical for sustaining long-term vision preservation.

---

## Introduction

Retinitis pigmentosa (RP) is a group of inherited retinal diseases characterized by progressive vision loss due to mutations in photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). More than 80 genes with over 3000 mutations have been linked to RP1. Gene therapy targeting specific mutations, such as RPE65, has been approved for treating RP patients2,3. Given the high genetic diversity of RP, pursuing a mutation-independent therapeutic strategy to slow disease progression and preserve vision is a logical and promising approach.

Stem cell-based therapies offer promising avenues for treating retinal degenerative diseases through two main strategies: cell replacement and preservation of host cells. Replacement therapies, such as RPE cell transplants for age-related macular degeneration (AMD), have shown mixed outcomes in animal models and clinical trials4. Similarly, photoreceptor transplants at the advanced stages of retinal degeneration have shown promising results in animal studies; however, establishing synaptic connections with host retinal cells remains challenging5,6. Therapies that target preservation of host retinal cells have employed various stem cells in both preclinical and clinical settings, including retinal progenitor cells (RPCs)7, mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs)8–10, and human neural progenitor cells (hNPCs)11–13. hNPCs have been tested in multiple preclinical models, including rd1 and USH2A mutant mice14,15, RGC-depleted glaucoma mice16, and spinal cord injury models17, where they consistently demonstrated neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects. Our preclinical studies demonstrate that hNPCs delivered to the subretinal space of animal models survive long-term, migrate extensively, and protect vision by providing trophic support, regulating immune response, and enhancing antioxidant defense mechanisms by upregulating Nrf212,18,19. These findings have led to the delivery of clinical-grade hNPCs (termed CNS10-NPC) to RP patients in an ongoing phase I/2a clinical trial (NCT04284293).

While stem cell-based therapies hold promise for retinal disease, long-term protection is compromised due to efficacy deterioration over time, as widely reported from both preclinical and clinical studies. Key questions remain about the behavior of grafted stem cells and the host retina in a progressively degenerative environment, including how grafted cells adapt to their environment, how preserved photoreceptors evolve over time, and how grafted stem cells interact with host retinal cells. Here, we investigated the changes in hNPCs and host retinal cells over time following subretinal injection into the Royal College of Surgeons (RCS) rat, a well-characterized model for retinal degeneration. Using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), along with histological and functional assessments, we analyzed transcriptomic remodeling and intercellular interactions between grafted hNPCs and host retinal cells. Fourteen hNPC subpopulations with distinct transcriptional states were identified, indicating dynamic changes in grafted cells over time. Top-regulated genes, including mesencephalic astrocyte-derived neurotrophic factor (MANF), myeloid-derived growth factor (MYDGF), midkine (MDK), and pleiotrophin (PTN), were identified in hNPCs. The host retina showed temporal changes in phototransduction, visual perception, glial responses, and metabolic processes. Grafted hNPCs protect vision through multiple modalities, including trophic factor release, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, metabolic regulation, and suppression of apoptosis, oxidative stress, and inflammation. Notably, the signaling interaction and strength between hNPCs and host retinal cells declined over time. These findings provide insight into the dynamic changes in grafted hNPCs and host retinal cells and highlight the importance of combining stem cell therapy with improving host retinal environment to sustain long-term vision preservation.
